subject: chemistry
title: Unit 2 practice exam
summary: An 80-minute exam-style test on all of Unit 2, with six short-answer questions and full worked solutions plus 20 multiple-choice questions on water, acids and bases, pH, redox, stoichiometry and water analysis.
body:
This practice exam tests everything in Year 11 Chemistry Unit 2, in the same style as a school exam: written questions where you show your working, and multiple-choice questions. Doing it under real conditions is the best way to find the topics you still need to work on.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 80 minutes in total. Spend about 50 minutes on the short-answer questions (40 marks) and about 30 minutes on the 20 multiple-choice questions (20 marks).
- **Conditions:** work alone, with no notes. You may use a scientific calculator, a periodic table and the VCE data book.
- **Use these values:** relative atomic masses H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Cl 35.5, Ca 40.1, Cu 63.5, Ag 107.9. Specific heat capacity of water c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Latent heat of fusion of water = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹; latent heat of vaporisation of water = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Molar volume of a gas at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa) = 24.8 L mol⁻¹. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
- Write your short answers on paper first, then mark them against the worked solutions. Show formulas, units and significant figures, because that is where marks are won and lost.
- Then do the multiple-choice questions below and read every explanation.
- Note the topics where you lost marks and revise those lessons.

## Topics covered

- Properties of water, specific heat capacity and latent heat
- Solubility, solubility tables and curves, precipitation and ionic equations
- Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases, conjugate pairs, strength and concentration
- pH calculations for strong acids and bases, Kw and dilution
- Redox reactions, oxidation numbers, half-equations, displacement and corrosion
- Concentration units (mol L⁻¹, g L⁻¹, ppm), dilution and stoichiometry, including gases at SLC and limiting reactants
- Gravimetric analysis, colorimetry, UV-visible spectroscopy, calibration curves and AAS
- Volumetric analysis (titrations) and primary standards
- Practical investigation skills: variables, accuracy, precision, errors and validity

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (6 marks)

A kettle contains 500 g of water at 15.0 °C.

a. Explain, in terms of bonding, why water has a much higher specific heat capacity than most other liquids. (2 marks)

b. Calculate the total energy, in kJ, needed to heat all of the water to 100.0 °C and then boil away 50.0 g of it. (3 marks)

c. Explain why ice floats on liquid water. (1 mark)

### Question 2 (7 marks)

To find the chloride content of a bore water sample, a student added excess silver nitrate solution to a 50.0 mL sample. The white precipitate was filtered, washed and dried to constant mass. Its mass was 0.287 g.

a. Write the net ionic equation, with states, for the formation of the precipitate. (1 mark)

b. Explain why the silver nitrate was added in excess. (1 mark)

c. Calculate the concentration of chloride ions in the sample in mol L⁻¹. (3 marks)

d. Express the chloride concentration in mg L⁻¹. (1 mark)

e. The student forgot to wash the precipitate. State and explain the effect on the calculated chloride concentration. (1 mark)

### Question 3 (7 marks)

Nitric acid, HNO₃, is a strong acid.

a. Write an equation for the reaction of nitric acid with water and identify both conjugate acid–base pairs. (2 marks)

b. Calculate the pH of 0.020 mol L⁻¹ HNO₃ at 25 °C. (1 mark)

c. 10.0 mL of this acid is diluted with water to a final volume of 1.00 L. Calculate the new pH. (2 marks)

d. Calculate the pH of 0.0250 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C. (2 marks)

### Question 4 (7 marks)

Acidified potassium permanganate solution (purple, containing MnO₄⁻) oxidises iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions. The permanganate is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺ ions.

a. Write the balanced reduction half-equation for MnO₄⁻ forming Mn²⁺ in acidic solution. (2 marks)

b. Write the oxidation half-equation. (1 mark)

c. Write the balanced overall equation. (1 mark)

d. Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. (1 mark)

e. A steel roof sheet is galvanised (coated with zinc). Explain why the steel does not rust even where the zinc coating is scratched. (2 marks)

### Question 5 (8 marks)

A student made a standard solution by dissolving 1.325 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, in deionised water and making it up to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. 20.00 mL aliquots of this solution were titrated with hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration.

`Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)`

| Titre | Rough | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of HCl (mL) | 22.30 | 21.65 | 21.60 | 21.70 | 21.95 |

a. Give one reason why anhydrous sodium carbonate is suitable as a primary standard. (1 mark)

b. Calculate the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution. (2 marks)

c. Identify the concordant titres and calculate the average titre. (1 mark)

d. Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid. (3 marks)

e. The equivalence point of this titration is at a pH below 7. Suggest a suitable indicator. (1 mark)

### Question 6 (5 marks)

The copper(II) ion concentration in waste water from a factory was measured by colorimetry. Standard solutions gave these results:

| Cu²⁺ concentration (mg L⁻¹) | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Absorbance | 0.00 | 0.12 | 0.24 | 0.36 | 0.48 |

A 10.0 mL sample of the waste water was diluted to 50.0 mL. The diluted solution had an absorbance of 0.30.

a. Explain why the colorimeter was set to the wavelength that Cu²⁺ absorbs most strongly (λmax). (1 mark)

b. Calculate the Cu²⁺ concentration in the original waste water in mg L⁻¹. (2 marks)

c. Another student used a scratched cuvette, which added 0.05 to every absorbance reading, including the standards measured in it. Name the type of error and state how it affects accuracy and precision. (2 marks)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a. Water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds (H bonded to O, attracted to a lone pair on a neighbouring O) (1 mark). When water is heated, much of the energy goes into stretching and breaking these hydrogen bonds rather than making the molecules move faster, so the temperature rises slowly and a lot of energy is needed per gram per degree (1 mark).

b. Step 1, heating 500 g from 15.0 °C to 100.0 °C (ΔT = 85.0 °C):

`q = m × c × ΔT = 500 × 4.18 × 85.0 = 177 650 J = 177.65 kJ` (1 mark)

Step 2, boiling 50.0 g:

`n(H₂O) = m ÷ M = 50.0 ÷ 18.0 = 2.778 mol`

`q = n × ΔH = 2.778 × 40.7 = 113.06 kJ` (1 mark)

Total: 177.65 + 113.06 = 290.71 kJ, so **291 kJ** (1 mark, three significant figures). Note that the boiling step needs almost as much energy as heating all the water by 85 °C.

c. In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice with a lot of empty space, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats (1 mark).

### Question 2

a. `Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)` (1 mark, states needed)

b. Excess silver ions make sure that all of the chloride ions are precipitated, so the mass of AgCl represents all the chloride in the sample (1 mark).

c. M(AgCl) = 107.9 + 35.5 = 143.4 g mol⁻¹

`n(AgCl) = 0.287 ÷ 143.4 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol` (1 mark)

Mole ratio Cl⁻ : AgCl = 1 : 1, so n(Cl⁻) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol (1 mark)

`c(Cl⁻) = n ÷ V = 2.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0500 = 0.0400 mol L⁻¹` (1 mark)

d. Mass concentration = c × M = 0.0400 × 35.5 = 1.42 g L⁻¹ = **1.42 × 10³ mg L⁻¹** (1 mark). Check: mass of Cl⁻ = 2.00 × 10⁻³ × 35.5 = 0.0710 g = 71.0 mg in 0.0500 L, and 71.0 ÷ 0.0500 = 1420 mg L⁻¹.

e. The result would be **too high**: unwashed precipitate still carries soluble impurities (such as sodium nitrate and excess silver nitrate), so the weighed mass is larger than the true mass of AgCl (1 mark).

### Question 3

a. `HNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) → NO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)` (1 mark). The arrow is one way because nitric acid ionises completely. Conjugate pairs: HNO₃/NO₃⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O (1 mark).

b. HNO₃ is a strong monoprotic acid, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.020 mol L⁻¹.

`pH = −log₁₀(0.020) = 1.70` (1 mark; two significant figures in the concentration give two decimal places)

c. `c₂ = c₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = (0.020 × 10.0) ÷ 1000 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹` (1 mark; both volumes in mL)

`pH = −log₁₀(2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.70` (1 mark). Check: a 100-fold dilution should raise the pH by 2 units, from 1.70 to 3.70.

d. NaOH is a strong base, so [OH⁻] = 0.0250 mol L⁻¹.

`[H₃O⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.0250 = 4.00 × 10⁻¹³ mol L⁻¹` (1 mark)

`pH = −log₁₀(4.00 × 10⁻¹³) = 12.40` (1 mark)

### Question 4

a. Use KOHES. Mn is already balanced; add 4H₂O to balance O; add 8H⁺ to balance H; add 5e⁻ to the left to balance charge (left: −1 + 8 = +7; right: +2).

`MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l)` (2 marks: 1 for correct species and atom balance, 1 for electrons and states)

b. `Fe²⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻` (1 mark)

c. Multiply the oxidation half-equation by 5 so that 5 electrons are lost and gained, then add:

`MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 5Fe³⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l)` (1 mark)

Check charge: left = −1 + 8 + 10 = +17; right = +2 + 15 = +17. Balanced.

d. Oxidising agent: MnO₄⁻ (it is reduced). Reducing agent: Fe²⁺ (it is oxidised). (1 mark for both)

e. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it is a stronger reducing agent and is oxidised in preference to iron (1 mark). Electrons from the zinc flow to the exposed iron, so the iron is not oxidised; the zinc acts as a sacrificial metal and is slowly used up instead (1 mark).

### Question 5

a. Any one (1 mark): it can be obtained in very high purity; it is stable and does not absorb water or carbon dioxide from the air (in its anhydrous form); it has a known formula; it has a fairly high molar mass, which reduces the percentage error in weighing.

b. M(Na₂CO₃) = 2(23.0) + 12.0 + 3(16.0) = 106.0 g mol⁻¹

`n(Na₂CO₃) = 1.325 ÷ 106.0 = 0.01250 mol` (1 mark)

`c(Na₂CO₃) = 0.01250 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.05000 mol L⁻¹` (1 mark)

c. Concordant titres are 21.65, 21.60 and 21.70 mL (within 0.10 mL of each other). The rough titre and 21.95 mL are left out. Average = (21.65 + 21.60 + 21.70) ÷ 3 = 64.95 ÷ 3 = **21.65 mL** (1 mark).

d. `n(Na₂CO₃) in aliquot = c × V = 0.05000 × 0.02000 = 1.000 × 10⁻³ mol` (1 mark)

`n(HCl) = 2 × 1.000 × 10⁻³ = 2.000 × 10⁻³ mol` (1 mark, using the 2 : 1 mole ratio)

`c(HCl) = 2.000 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.02165 = 0.09238 mol L⁻¹` (1 mark, four significant figures)

e. **Methyl orange** (1 mark). It changes colour in an acidic pH range, matching an equivalence point below 7 (the reaction of a strong acid with a weak base, carbonate).

### Question 6

a. At λmax the analyte absorbs the most light, so the change in absorbance per unit of concentration is largest (greatest sensitivity), and interference from other substances is reduced (1 mark).

b. From the calibration data, absorbance rises by 0.12 for every 20 mg L⁻¹, which is 0.0060 per mg L⁻¹.

`Diluted concentration = 0.30 ÷ 0.0060 = 50 mg L⁻¹` (1 mark; reading 50 mg L⁻¹ from a graph is also fine)

The sample was diluted from 10.0 mL to 50.0 mL, a dilution factor of 50.0 ÷ 10.0 = 5.0.

`Original concentration = 50 × 5.0 = 250 mg L⁻¹` (1 mark)

c. It is a **systematic error**, because every reading is shifted by the same amount in the same direction (1 mark). It reduces accuracy (results are further from the true value) but does not affect precision, because repeat readings are still close to each other (1 mark).

questions.prompt: How much energy is needed to melt 36.0 g of ice at 0 °C? (Latent heat of fusion = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹; M(H₂O) = 18.0 g mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation: n = 36.0 ÷ 18.0 = 2.00 mol, so q = n × ΔH = 2.00 × 6.01 = 12.0 kJ. Option C multiplies the mass in grams by the molar value (36.0 × 6.01), but ΔH is per mole, not per gram. Option D uses the latent heat of vaporisation, which is for boiling, not melting.

questions.prompt: Using solubility rules, which compound is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: Carbonates are insoluble except with Na⁺, K⁺ and NH₄⁺, so zinc carbonate is insoluble. Option A is tempting because phosphates are usually insoluble, but sodium compounds are always soluble. All nitrates are soluble, so B is soluble.

questions.prompt: The solubility of potassium nitrate is 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 32 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. A saturated solution containing 50 g of water at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. What mass of potassium nitrate crystallises?
questions.explanation: Per 100 g of water, 110 − 32 = 78 g would crystallise. With only 50 g of water, the amounts are halved: 78 ÷ 2 = 39 g. Option A is the tempting answer that forgets the solution contains only 50 g of water, not 100 g.

questions.prompt: Lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution and a yellow precipitate forms. Which ions are spectator ions?
questions.explanation: The precipitate is PbI₂ (iodides are insoluble with Pb²⁺). K⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay dissolved and unchanged, so they are spectator ions. Option A lists the ions that form the precipitate, which are the ones that actually react.

questions.prompt: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: A conjugate base has one fewer H⁺ than its acid, so removing one proton from H₂PO₄⁻ gives HPO₄²⁻ (the charge drops by 1). Option B is the conjugate acid (one H⁺ added). Option C removes two protons.

questions.prompt: What are the products when magnesium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?

options.D: Magnesium sulfate, water and carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: A reactive metal and an acid give a salt and hydrogen gas: Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g). Option A is the pattern for an acid with a hydroxide or oxide, and option D is the pattern for an acid with a carbonate.

questions.prompt: Solution X has a pH of 3 and solution Y has a pH of 5. How does [H₃O⁺] in X compare with [H₃O⁺] in Y?
questions.explanation: Each pH unit is a tenfold change in [H₃O⁺]. X is 2 units lower, so its [H₃O⁺] is 10 × 10 = 100 times greater (10⁻³ compared with 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹). Option A treats the pH scale as linear rather than logarithmic.

questions.prompt: What is [OH⁻] in a solution with a pH of 4.00 at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁴·⁰⁰ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Using Kw, [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol L⁻¹. Option B is [H₃O⁺], not [OH⁻]. Option D is only true for neutral water.

questions.prompt: A 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution of hydrochloric acid (pH 1.0) is diluted 1000-fold. What is the new pH?
questions.explanation: A 1000-fold dilution lowers [H₃O⁺] from 0.10 to 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹, so the pH rises by 3 units, from 1.0 to 4.0. Option C forgets that the starting pH was 1.0, not 0. The pH of an acid cannot go above 7 by dilution, so D is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a redox reaction?
questions.explanation: Sodium goes from 0 to +1 (oxidised) and chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (reduced), so electrons are transferred. In A, B and D no oxidation numbers change: they are precipitation and acid–base reactions. Option D is tempting because a gas forms, but carbon stays at +4.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct half-equation for the oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfate ions in acidic solution?
questions.explanation: Two H₂O balance the oxygen (2 + 2 = 4 O), four H⁺ balance the hydrogen, and the charges must match: left side 0, right side −2 + 4 = +2, so 2e⁻ go on the right, giving 0 on both sides. Electrons are products in an oxidation. Option A puts the electrons on the wrong side, and option C has the wrong number of electrons (the charges do not balance).

questions.prompt: Blocks of zinc are attached to the steel hull of a ship. Why does this protect the hull from corrosion?

options.A: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it is oxidised instead of the iron.
options.B: Zinc is less reactive than iron, so it does not corrode.
options.C: Zinc forms a barrier that covers the whole hull.
options.D: Zinc reduces the amount of oxygen in seawater.

questions.explanation: This is sacrificial protection: zinc is the stronger reducing agent, so it loses electrons in preference to iron and is slowly used up while the iron stays unchanged. Option C describes barrier protection, but the blocks only cover small parts of the hull; they work through their reactivity, not by covering it.

questions.prompt: What mass of sodium hydroxide (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) is needed to make 250.0 mL of a 0.200 mol L⁻¹ solution?
questions.explanation: n = c × V = 0.200 × 0.2500 = 0.0500 mol, and m = n × M = 0.0500 × 40.0 = 2.00 g. Option A ignores the volume (it is the mass for 1.00 L). Option B uses the volume in mL instead of converting it to litres.

questions.prompt: A 500 mL water sample contains 2.5 mg of lead. What is the lead concentration in ppm? (Assume 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg L⁻¹.)
questions.explanation: Concentration = 2.5 mg ÷ 0.500 L = 5.0 mg L⁻¹ ≈ 5.0 ppm. Option A multiplies by 0.500 instead of dividing. Option C ignores the volume, but ppm is a concentration, so it must be per litre.

questions.prompt: 0.30 mol of aluminium reacts with 0.60 mol of chlorine gas: `2Al(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2AlCl₃(s)`. Which reactant is limiting, and how many moles of AlCl₃ form?
questions.explanation: Divide each amount by its coefficient: Al 0.30 ÷ 2 = 0.15; Cl₂ 0.60 ÷ 3 = 0.20. Al gives the smaller value, so it is limiting. n(AlCl₃) = n(Al) × 2/2 = 0.30 mol (only 0.45 mol of Cl₂ is used). Option B comes from assuming Cl₂ runs out first (0.60 × 2/3 = 0.40 mol AlCl₃), but that would need 0.40 mol of Al, and only 0.30 mol is available.

questions.prompt: A 20.00 mL aliquot of sulfuric acid is titrated with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ NaOH, and the average titre is 18.00 mL. `H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)`. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.01800 = 1.800 × 10⁻³ mol. n(H₂SO₄) = 1.800 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2 = 9.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol. c = 9.00 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.02000 = 0.0450 mol L⁻¹. Option A forgets the 1 : 2 mole ratio. Option B swaps the two volumes.

questions.prompt: Why is solid sodium hydroxide not used as a primary standard?

options.A: It is a strong base and reacts too quickly.
options.B: Its molar mass is too large.
options.C: It absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so its mass and composition change.
options.D: It does not dissolve in water.

questions.explanation: A primary standard must be weighed accurately and have a known composition. NaOH absorbs moisture and reacts with CO₂ from the air, so a weighed sample is not pure NaOH. Option B is wrong: a high molar mass is actually an advantage for a primary standard, and NaOH's is quite low (40.0 g mol⁻¹).

questions.prompt: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid (a weak acid) with sodium hydroxide (a strong base)?

options.A: Methyl orange, because it changes colour in acidic solution
options.B: Phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is above pH 7
options.C: Any indicator, because all acid–base titrations end at pH 7
options.D: Methyl orange, because the acid is weak

questions.explanation: A weak acid with a strong base gives a slightly basic solution at the equivalence point, so phenolphthalein, which changes colour above pH 7, is chosen. Option C is a common misconception: only strong acid–strong base titrations have an equivalence point near pH 7.

questions.prompt: A student repeats a titration and obtains titres of 24.10, 24.12 and 24.08 mL. The true titre is known to be 23.50 mL. What do these results show?

options.A: They are accurate and precise; there is no error.
options.B: They are precise but not accurate, suggesting a systematic error.
options.C: They are accurate but not precise, suggesting random errors.
options.D: They are neither accurate nor precise.

questions.explanation: The three titres are very close to each other (precise), but all are about 0.6 mL above the true value (not accurate). A consistent shift in one direction points to a systematic error, such as an incorrectly calibrated burette or poor rinsing. Option C has the two terms the wrong way around.

questions.prompt: In atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), why is the lamp made of the same element that is being measured?

options.A: So that the lamp heats the sample to a high enough temperature to atomise it
options.B: So that the element can be seen glowing in the flame
options.C: So that the sample dissolves in the solvent more easily
options.D: So that the light emitted has exactly the wavelengths that only atoms of that element absorb

questions.explanation: Atoms of each element absorb light only at certain specific wavelengths. A lamp made of the same element emits exactly those wavelengths, so only that element absorbs, making AAS very selective. Option A is tempting, but the flame atomises the sample; the lamp only provides light.
